q: My bad commit is already pushed, and my team pulled it. Do I use reset or revert?
expl: Revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody's history breaks. Reset rewrites history.
ch: 5. Undo a shared commit: git revert
opts: git reset --hard HEAD~1
git revert HEAD
git restore

q: I ran git reset --hard and the commit vanished. Is it gone for good?
expl: Not right away. `git reflog` still lists it, and you can reset back to it.
ch: 4. Drop a commit with reset --hard, then get it back
opts: Yes, reset --hard deletes it at once
No: git reflog still lists it, and you can reset back
Only if it was never pushed

q: You added a bad line to `app.conf` and haven't committed. Type the `git restore` command that puts the file back to the last committed version.
expl: `git restore <file>` copies the last committed version over your edit. The status is clean again.
ch: 1. Throw away an edit: git restore

q: You ran `git add app.conf` too early. Type the `git restore` command that takes it out of the staging area but keeps your edit in the file.
expl: `--staged` only touches the staging area. Without it, restore works on the file itself.

q: You ran `git restore app.conf` on an edit you never committed. Can git bring that edit back?
expl: Restore overwrites the file, and an edit that was never committed (or added) isn't stored anywhere in git.
ch: 1. Throw away an edit: git restore
opts: Yes, with `git reflog`
No: git never had a copy of it, so it's gone
Yes, with `git restore --staged app.conf`

expl: The commit is gone from the log, but its change stays in the file (and staged), ready to be committed again.

q: Type the command that removes the last commit from the branch but keeps its changes staged, so you can commit them again.
expl: `--soft` only moves the branch back; the index and your files keep the changes. `HEAD~1`, `HEAD~` and `HEAD^` all mean the parent commit.
ch: 3. Undo the last commit, keep the changes: reset --soft

q: You have an uncommitted edit in `app.conf` and run `git reset --hard HEAD~1`. Later you reset back to `HEAD@{1}`. Is your edit back too?
expl: Reset --hard also wipes uncommitted changes, and git never stored them. Run `git status` before you use it.
ch: 4. Drop a commit with reset --hard, then get it back
opts: Yes, reset --hard never touches uncommitted changes
No: reflog brings back the commit, but the uncommitted edit is gone
Yes, the edit is saved in the reflog together with the commit

expl: Nothing is deleted: the original commit stays, and a new “Revert …” commit undoes its change.
ch: 5. Undo a shared commit: git revert
opts: Deletes the last commit from history
Adds a new commit that does the opposite of the last one

q: After `git restore --staged app.conf`, `git status --short` shows `M` in the second column. What does that mean?
expl: First column = staged, second column = changed in your working folder but not staged yet.
opts: The change is staged and ready to commit
The file is modified, but the change is not staged
The file was merged from another branch
